questions.q: Describe the different types of markets and how they differ.
answer: We buy goods and services from many kinds of markets, which differ in cost and convenience.

answer.text: Held on a fixed day of the week, they have no permanent shops, so costs are low and goods are cheaper and open to bargaining.
Permanent shops close to home are convenient, familiar, and often sell on credit.
These house many shops selling branded goods and are usually more expensive.
People can now buy from home, with goods delivered to them. Some markets sell directly to consumers (retail) and others in bulk to shopkeepers (wholesale).

questions.q: Explain the chain of markets from producer to consumer.
answer: Most goods pass through a chain of markets before they reach us.

answer.text: A wholesaler buys goods in large quantities directly from producers and sells them to retailers. Buying in bulk allows the wholesaler to get lower prices.
A retailer buys smaller quantities from the wholesaler and sells them to the final consumer in the shop or market.
So the usual chain runs from the producer to the wholesaler, then to the retailer, and finally to the consumer, with the price rising at each step.
The gains are shared unequally along this chain — big traders often profit more than the producer or the small seller.

questions.q: How does a weekly market differ from shops in a neighbourhood and a shopping mall?
answer: We buy goods from many kinds of markets, which differ in where they are held, who sells and what they offer.

answer.text: A weekly market is held on a fixed day of the week in an open space. It has no permanent shops; traders set up stalls in the morning and pack up in the evening. Goods are cheaper because sellers have low costs and bargaining is common, but the choice is limited.
Shops in a neighbourhood are permanent and open on most days, close to where people live, and useful for daily needs, though their prices are usually fixed.
A shopping mall is a large, air-conditioned building with many branded shops selling costly goods, visited mostly by better-off customers.

answer: Thus weekly markets are cheap and temporary, neighbourhood shops are handy and permanent, and malls are large and expensive.

questions.q: Why do markets not offer equal benefits to everyone?

answer.text: The many kinds of markets do not treat all people equally, because buyers and sellers differ greatly in their wealth and power.

A rich person can shop in costly malls and buy branded goods, while a poor person can afford only cheaper goods from a weekly market or a small shop. So people's spending depends on how much money they have.

Among sellers too there is inequality. A big businessman or factory owner earns large profits, while a small hawker or a weekly-market trader earns very little despite hard work. The small producer and the poor buyer are the weakest in the chain.

answer: Thus markets favour those with more money and power, so their benefits are not shared equally among buyers and sellers.
